hinder

/HIN-der/ - the stress falls on HIN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Hinder means to make progress harder — to slow, complicate, or set something back without necessarily stopping it altogether.

Fog hindered the search teams all morning, shrinking every sweep of the hillside to arm's length.

Example

The expedition's real enemy was not the cold but the stamps: every border crossing demanded new paperwork, and each delay hindered the climbers just enough that they reached base camp three weeks behind the weather window.

Hinder names friction, not a wall. The climbers were never stopped — they were slowed, complicated, and set back, which is exactly the word's range: making progress harder while it continues. When something is halted outright, hinder understates it; when it merely arrives late but whole, hinder overstates it. The word's home is the costly middle.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hamper: To hamper is to restrict movement as if something were tangled around you — you are hampered by a heavy coat, by wet rope, by regulations that bind. Hinder is the broader word for any drag on progress, and it points at the result: a hindered effort ends up behind.

impede: To impede is to slow something by putting an obstacle in its path — the word comes from Latin for shackling the feet. Hinder needs no obstacle in the road at all: fatigue, red tape, or plain bad luck can hinder you, because hinder measures the setback, not the barrier.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

facilitate: to make a process easier or smoother

expedite: to speed an action along

Where it sits · how much of the progress is taken away

delay → hinder → thwart

delay vs. hinder: To delay is milder than to hinder: a delayed shipment arrives whole, just later, while a hindered one loses ground the whole way — slowed, complicated, and set back at every turn.

thwart vs. hinder: To thwart goes further than to hinder: a hindered plan still limps toward the finish, but a thwarted one is defeated outright — the goal is never reached at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hind: back, behind (Old English — the same hind of hindsight and a horse's hind legs)

Suffix — -er: verb-forming ending (Old English -rian)

Put it together: Hind (back, behind) + -er (verb-forming) = to put behind, to hold to the rear. Old English hindrian meant to keep someone back — literally to be-hind their progress. A hindrance is not a wall across the road; it is the drag that keeps a mover from getting ahead.

Use the root in a new word: hindsight: In hindsight, the detour that wrecked our schedule turned out to be the best part of the trip.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, slightly formal

Hinder is the measured word for friction against progress — at home in reports, rulings, and post-game explanations. It takes a direct object: rain hinders the harvest, debt hinders the recovery. Reach for block or prevent when the thing never happens at all; hinder promises only difficulty and lost ground while the effort goes on. In this unit, forestall acts early, before trouble starts — hinder drags at something already underway.
